messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 60
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Hotel Manager
- Trauma Type: Toxic chemical exposure
- Pcl5: 68

He is a man who once moved through the lobby with a quiet authority, greeting guests by name, smoothing over problems before they became complaints. Now, at sixty, he finds himself constantly scanning, not for dissatisfied customers, but for the air itself. He has been the hotel manager for twenty-three years, and for the last two of those years, he has not set foot in the housekeeping supply closet on the third floor.

The event happened on a Tuesday afternoon, during the off-season when the hotel was half-empty. He had been asked to inspect a room on the fourth floor where a guest had complained about a strange smell. Maintenance had already checked the HVAC, so he went himself. The smell was sharp, chemical, almost sweet. He opened the door and felt it hit his face like a warm, oily film. A small valve on a cleaning solution dispenser in the bathroom had cracked, and a fine mist of concentrated hydrogen peroxide-based disinfectant had been leaking into the room for hours. The window was sealed shut. He was inside for no more than three minutes, but that was enough.

That night, his throat burned. His eyes watered, and he coughed until his ribs ached. The urgent care doctor said it was irritation, gave him a nebulizer, told him he would be fine. But the cough never fully stopped. For weeks, he woke up gasping, his lungs feeling like they were lined with sandpaper. When he returned to work, the hotel insisted on replacing the chemical supply with a different brand. They had training sessions. They put up signs. But he could not stop thinking about the moment when the mist touched his face, the helplessness of not being able to leave because he had to make sure the room was safe for the next guest.

Now, every time he walks past the housekeeping cart in the hallway, he holds his breath. He has learned to exhale slowly through his mouth when he passes anyone wearing gloves or holding a spray bottle. If a guest asks for an extra cleaning, he delegates it immediately, making an excuse about a meeting. He cannot explain why his hands start trembling when he sees the word “disinfectant” on a label. He cannot tell his partner, who has started to comment on his irritability, that when she uses oven cleaner at home, he has to leave the apartment and stand on the fire escape until his heart stops pounding.

At work, he has developed a habit of checking the fire alarm systems, the sprinklers, the air vents. He schedules extra inspections himself, even when his staff says it is unnecessary. He has become the manager who is always watching, always ready for a leak, a spill, a silent poison. His colleagues call him meticulous. The general manager calls him overly cautious. He just feels tired.

He no longer enjoys going out to restaurants, because the smell of bleach in the bathroom stall can trigger a wave of nausea and a rushing sense of doom. He avoids crowded indoor spaces where he cannot see the exits. He has lost interest in cooking, because he cannot stand the scent of vinegar or ammonia. His partner has noticed that he sleeps in a separate room now, because he sometimes thrashes awake from dreams where he is trapped in a sealed white room, gasping for air that tastes like metal.

He thinks about the three minutes often. He replays them. He wonders if he should have worn a mask, if he should have waited for maintenance, if the damage is invisible and permanent. The doctors say his lungs are clear, but his body does not believe them. His body still remembers the mist, and it is always waiting for it to return.
